text: Every box is scanned at the door.
The batch was dispatched at six this morning.
The shipment has been cleared by customs.
Forty trucks are loaded every night.
So, Marcelo, what happens when a batch of vaccines arrives here?
First, every box is scanned at the door. Then it is stored in the cold room, at two to eight degrees.
And who checks the temperature? Is it done by hand?
Not anymore. The temperature is recorded every five minutes, and if anything changes, the pallet is flagged automatically.
What was the biggest bottleneck when you started here?
The hand-off to the carriers. Trucks were held up for hours at the gate. We have streamlined the process since then.
And if a medicine has a problem after it leaves the building?
Then a recall is started. Every box can be traced to the minute. Traceability is our safety net.
The shipment was held up at the port.
It has been cleared by customs.
I made the decision, and I will fix it.

Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. Thank you again for the tour of the distribution center yesterday. My editor has already read the first draft, and she loved it. I have just two questions before I finish. I wrote that the vaccines are kept at two to eight degrees, but are they checked again before they are dispatched? And the shipment that was held up at the port on Tuesday, has it been cleared yet? One more thing. You told me that nothing is done by hand anymore. My readers will love that line, but I need to be sure it is true. I would like to send the piece to my editor on Friday, so call me when you can.

Welcome back to The Long Game. Today, a grammar point that every manager uses and almost nobody notices: the passive. Listen to two sentences. Our team dispatched the order at six. The order was dispatched at six. Same fact, different focus. In the first sentence, the hero is the team. In the second, the hero is the order. When you describe a process, the object is usually more important than the person, so the passive sounds natural. The boxes are scanned, the trucks are loaded, the batch has been released. But be careful, because the passive can also be used to hide. Mistakes were made. By whom? If you are the director and something went wrong, say who did it, especially if it was you. That is what people trust. So here is the rule for this week: use the passive for processes, and the active for responsibility.

First, the batch is received and every box is scanned. Then, it is stored in the cold room at two to eight degrees. Next, the temperature is recorded every five minutes. After that, the order is checked and loaded onto a truck. Finally, the batch is dispatched to the pharmacies.
Every box is scanned at the door.
The shipment was held up at the port.
It has been cleared by customs.
If the temperature changes, the pallet is flagged automatically.
Our lead time is three days, from order to pharmacy.
I made the decision, and I will fix it.
